wave: CORRECTNESS -- the ADL constraint parser located where/require/require-materialized keywords via naive substring search, letting an ordinary declared attribute name (elsewhere, requires_review) corrupt or silently drop a constraint clause
wave_title: Seventh fix this generation cycle. After closing the CLI argument-parsing gap, pivoted to a fresh area (ADL compiler, identity, docs/source inventory, temporal/provenance, semantic dimension identity_key() methods) via a scoped Explore survey to avoid over-mining the four files already hardened this cycle. The survey's single reported finding was independently re-verified against real code, including reconstructing both failure modes as executable tests, before any change.
priority_classification: correctness/architectural integrity -- highest category in the standing priority order. A real, silent semantic corruption of a user's own declared constraint, reachable via ordinary English attribute names (not adversarial input), that can flip a real `atlas-cli check`/`systemize` pass/fail outcome with zero diagnostic.
gap_discovered_by: Delegated Explore subagent survey, explicitly scoped to files untouched by this cycle's six prior fixes (ADL compiler, identity, docs/source inventory walkers, temporal/provenance, and every semantic dimension's identity_key() method). Its single reported finding was independently re-verified before any change: read parse_constraint_check's where/require/require-materialized handling directly (not from the subagent's paraphrase), confirmed the exact naive-substring-split code shape, then independently reconstructed both claimed failure modes as real executable tests against the actual unfixed code (not merely trusted the subagent's described output) -- both reproduced exactly as reported.
key_finding: parse_constraint_check located the `where`/`require`/`require materialized` keywords via plain `str::split("where")`/`str::split("require")` on the raw joined constraint-body text, rather than exact whole-word matching. Any declared ADL attribute name that merely CONTAINS one of these keywords as a substring -- `elsewhere`, `requires_review`, `required_by`, all ordinary, plausible real-world attribute names, not adversarial input -- collided with the keyword search. Two distinct failure modes, both independently reproduced: (1) an attribute containing "require" (e.g. `requires_review`) corrupts require-clause splitting, causing a syntactically valid constraint to be rejected as unrecognized (ATLAS-E052 + ATLAS-E053, `checks` empty); (2) an attribute containing "where" (e.g. `elsewhere`) causes the where-filter to silently resolve to `None` with ZERO diagnostic -- since `where_attr`/`where_value` are `Option` fields not required for the overall constraint match to succeed, `constraint.checks` still gets built but silently means "require ALL entities of this kind satisfy require_attr == require_value" instead of the user's actual, narrower "require entities WHERE where_attr == where_value satisfy require_attr == require_value" -- a real, silent semantic change to the compiled constraint that can flip `constraint_results`/`atlas-cli check`'s pass/fail outcome for a perfectly valid `.adl` file.
verification_before_acting: Read parse_constraint_check's real, current code directly (lines 387-431 before the fix) confirming the exact naive str::split usage the subagent described.

Read the ConstraintCheck::AttributeEquals evaluation logic (the `if let (Some(attr), Some(value)) = (where_attr, where_value) ... continue` filter) directly, confirming that where_attr == None genuinely means the filter never triggers -- so ALL entities of the kind get checked, not zero -- exactly matching the claimed silent semantic-widening consequence, not merely an omission.

Independently reconstructed BOTH claimed failure modes as real, executable tests against the actual unfixed code (not just trusted the subagent's described terminal output) -- both reproduced exactly: the requires_review case really does produce ATLAS-E052 with an empty checks list; the elsewhere case really does produce a checks entry with where_attr: None, where_value: None instead of the attribute's real values.
Confirmed via grep that no existing test in this file exercised a keyword-substring collision before this generation.

design_decisions.question: Patch the where/require split with an ad hoc guard, or restructure the search to be genuinely word-boundary-safe?
design_decisions.decision: Restructured to operate on the same `words: Vec<&str>` whitespace-token list `entity_kind`'s own parsing already uses (`words.windows(3).find(...)`), locating `where`/`require` via `words.iter().position(|word| *word == "where")` (exact whole-word match) instead of `joined.split("where")` (substring match). This is the same fix shape `entity_kind`'s own parsing already used successfully -- extending an existing, already-correct pattern in this file to the two spots that hadn't adopted it, not inventing a new parsing strategy. Also fixed the `require materialized` two-word phrase the same way (`words.windows(2).position(|pair| pair[0] == "require" && pair[1] == "materialized")`), closing the same defect class there even though it's lower-severity (a two-word phrase is far less likely to collide with a real attribute name).

stable_validator_law_compliance.claim: parse_constraint_check now locates where/require/require-materialized keywords by exact whole-word match against the constraint body's token list, never by substring search against the raw text -- closing both the silent semantic-corruption (where-filter dropped) and false-rejection (valid constraint diagnosed as unrecognized) failure modes for any declared attribute name that happens to contain a keyword as a substring.
stable_validator_law_compliance.self_written_evidence: Added two new tests, each independently reconstructing one of the two reported failure modes as a real parse_adl_source call against real ADL source text: a_require_clause_attribute_name_containing_require_as_a_substring_still_parses (a `where x.requires_review == true` clause, asserting zero ATLAS-E052 diagnostics and the exact expected AttributeEquals check) and a_where_clause_attribute_name_containing_where_as_a_substring_is_not_silently_dropped (a `where x.elsewhere == true` clause, asserting the where_attr/where_value are preserved rather than silently None). Falsified per this session's standing discipline: backed up the file, reverted the fix to the original naive-substring-split code, ran both new tests, confirmed both failed with the EXACT reported failure modes verbatim (the requires_review test's failure output shows the real ATLAS-E052 diagnostic with the corrupted snippet; the elsewhere test's failure output shows where_attr: None, where_value: None instead of the real attribute), then restored the fix from backup (git diff --stat confirmed the restored file exactly matched the fix) and confirmed both tests pass.
